Flame_Spread_Measurement: N/A (Droplet combustion kinetics, not surface spread)
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus, UV/visible radiometers, color video
Key_Findings: Heptane droplets exhibited two-stage combustion: after visible hot flame extinction, a low-temperature cool flame continued burning invisibly, consuming fuel without buoyant convective heat loss.
AI_Research_Summary: NASA researchers discovered that liquid fuel droplets in microgravity can sustain invisible cool flames (below 1000 K) that continue burning without a visible flame envelope after apparent extinction.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Demonstrates that visual extinction does not guarantee a fire is out; spacecraft fire detection must monitor chemical gas species and infrared emissions rather than visible flame light alone.
Source_Notes: Published in Combustion and Flame 2014. Droplet burning rate K and extinction diameter measured; surface flame spread is not applicable to droplet experiments.

Flame_Spread_Measurement: ~18.0 mm/s (cotton-fiberglass surface spread in 20 cm/s flow)
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Thermocouple array, calibrated radiometers, high-resolution video
Key_Findings: Large-scale 0.4 m x 1.0 m cotton-fiberglass sample burned rapidly in low-speed forced airflow inside an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle, demonstrating that microgravity upward flame spread can exceed standard 1-g ground test expectations under ventilation.
AI_Research_Summary: The first large-scale fire test inside an actual space vehicle showed that fabrics burn vigorously in low-speed cabin ventilation currents, propagating flames faster than predicted by Earth-based upward tests.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Directly influenced spacecraft design: large exposed fabric surfaces in high-airflow cabin corridors represent high-risk propagation paths; automated ventilation shutdown upon smoke alarm is critical.
Source_Notes: AIAA 2017-3746. First test of the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project on Cygnus OA-6 after departure from ISS.

Fuel_Type: Mixed Solid Materials (Nomex, PMMA, Cotton, Silicone)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Evaluated NASA-STD-6001 materials in microgravity flow
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Video camera suite, thermocouple grid, radiant heat flux sensors
Key_Findings: Tested nine different spacecraft materials of various thicknesses under microgravity forced airflow; silicone-coated Nomex self-extinguished consistently, while cotton-fiberglass composites burned readily.
AI_Research_Summary: Evaluated whether materials approved by standard Earth flammability tests behave safely in space. Confirmed that flame-retardant materials like Nomex perform well, but thin fabrics burn readily under airflow.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Validates aerospace material screening while highlighting that materials passing 1-g pass/fail tests must still be restricted in total surface area in ventilated cabin ducts.
Source_Notes: Flew on Cygnus OA-5 in late 2016. Saffire-II used a multi-sample card with 9 distinct material strips.

Flame_Spread_Measurement: ~16.0 mm/s at 20 cm/s; lower spread at 10 cm/s
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Calibrated video tracking, airflow velocity sensors, radiometers
Key_Findings: Increasing forced airflow velocity approximately doubled the flame spread rate across the 1-meter fabric sample, confirming that spacecraft ventilation velocity is a primary driver of fire growth in microgravity.
AI_Research_Summary: Demonstrated that flame growth rate in microgravity is directly linked to ventilation speed: doubling the airflow velocity roughly doubled how fast the fire spread along the fabric.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Proves that cabin life-support fans actively feed flame propagation; spacecraft emergency procedures must balance isolating ventilation to starve fires against maintaining air scrubbers for crew breathing.
Source_Notes: Flew on Cygnus OA-7 in June 2017. Saffire-III re-tested Saffire-I geometry with varied airflow velocity.

Airflow_Conditions: Forced airflow ~15 cm/s, reduced pressure 65.5 kPa
Flame_Spread_Measurement: Smoldering & flame spread observed at elevated O2
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Smoldering persisted longer at elevated O2
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Tunable diode laser spectrometers (CO, CO2, HCN, HF), video
Key_Findings: Elevated oxygen concentration (26.5% exploration atmosphere) significantly increased ignition propensity and toxic gas production (CO, HCN) during smoldering and burning combustion of Nomex and PMMA samples.
AI_Research_Summary: Studied fire behavior in exploration atmospheres planned for Moon and Mars missions (higher oxygen percentage at lower total atmospheric pressure). Found increased ignition ease and elevated toxic gas release.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Critical for Artemis and Lunar Gateway: higher oxygen concentrations (up to 34% in airlocks) lower the ignition threshold of cabin materials and require enhanced toxic-gas scrubbing capacity.
Source_Notes: Flew on Cygnus NG-18 in late 2022. First Saffire flight dedicated to exploration atmospheres and toxic gas diagnostics.

Airflow_Conditions: Airflow 0 to 55 cm/s in flow duct
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Flames survived down to 17.0% O2 with airflow
Key_Findings: Thin PMMA fuel samples burned in microgravity down to 17% ambient oxygen when supported by forced airflow (5–15 cm/s). Flame spread depended strongly on flow velocity and sample width, showing that ventilation sustains burning below standard atmospheric oxygen levels.
AI_Research_Summary: Proved that small solid fires in microgravity can keep burning down to 17% oxygen if gentle air currents are present. In still air without flow, flames tended toward extinction due to lack of oxygen diffusion.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Counteracts the common misconception that microgravity fires readily self-extinguish; ventilation airflow feeds oxygen to the flame base, requiring active suppression rather than relying solely on quiescent starvation.
Source_Notes: BASS conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on ISS Expeditions 34/35. Published in 51st AIAA Aerospace Sciences 2013.

Experiment_Name: BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids II)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Narrow burning regime near extinction limits
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Dual-angle digital video, radiometers, flow anemometers
Key_Findings: Thick solid fuels require sustained external heat flux to maintain burning in microgravity and exhibit narrow burning regimes; self-extinction can occur at low airflow but is not guaranteed across all geometries and oxygen levels.
AI_Research_Summary: Investigated thick plastic components (like structural electronics covers). Because thick materials require significant heat to vaporize, they burn more slowly and are easier to extinguish, but still persist near airflow ducts.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Informs spacecraft materials selection: thick, dense polymer structural geometries are substantially more flame-resistant in microgravity than thin plastic films or packaging.
Source_Notes: Published in Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 2014. Follow-up to BASS focusing on fuel thickness and flame extinction limits.

Airflow_Conditions: Quiescent to low co-flow inside CIR
Flame_Spread_Measurement: N/A (Gaseous diffusion flame, not surface spread)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Measured extinction strain rates and O2 limits
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR high-speed imaging, color cameras, photomultipliers, gas chromatography
Key_Findings: Spherical diffusion flames in microgravity exhibited lower soot radiation losses, enabling stable burning near extinction limits with minimal visible luminosity across methane and ethylene burner flames.
AI_Research_Summary: Studied gas-phase diffusion flames in microgravity without buoyant convection. Discovered that gaseous flames remain stable at lower oxygen concentrations and with far less visible light than on Earth.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Demonstrates that gas leaks in spacecraft propulsion or life-support lines can sustain almost invisible flames at low oxygen levels; optical flame detectors must be supplemented with ultrasonic leak detectors.
Source_Notes: Suite of 6 microgravity investigations (BRE, s-FORTH, E-FIELD, etc.) operated in the CIR on ISS from 2017 through 2022.

Experiment_Name: BRE (Burning Rate Emulator, part of ACME)
Airflow_Conditions: Low co-flow inside CIR combustion chamber
Flame_Spread_Measurement: N/A (Porous burner gas emulation, not surface spread)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Measured burning rates and radiation at extinction
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR radiometers, gas analysis, high-resolution cameras
Key_Findings: Simulated the burning of solid and liquid materials using a flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel to measure burning rates, radiation, and extinction limits in microgravity without the complication of solid fuel pyrolysis.
AI_Research_Summary: Used a specialized porous gas burner to emulate how solids and liquids burn in microgravity, isolating the gas-phase flame physics from the melting and bubbling of solid materials.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Provides foundational burning-rate physics data used to validate computer fire-simulation codes for future spacecraft compartments without risking large-scale vehicle fires.
Source_Notes: Sub-investigation of the ACME package in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS, operating between 2017 and 2021.

Flame_Spread_Measurement: N/A (Droplet combustion kinetics, not surface spread)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Observed low-temperature oxidation without hot flame
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus, IR sensors, imaging
Key_Findings: Extended cool-flame droplet burning regimes were confirmed for heavy hydrocarbon surrogates, demonstrating sustained low-temperature oxidation without visible soot or hot flame luminosity.
AI_Research_Summary: Confirmed that heavier hydrocarbon fuels also produce persistent, invisible cool flames in space, sustaining chemical reactions for tens of seconds without emitting visible light.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Warns spacecraft payload engineers handling liquid hydrocarbon coolants or fuels that smoldering or flameless liquid oxidation can occur invisibly, generating toxic vapors without triggering traditional optical fire alarms.
Source_Notes: Operated in the CIR on ISS in 2018 as a follow-up to FLEX, extending cool-flame studies to heavier n-alkane liquid fuels.

Fuel_Type: Solid Fabric & Polymer (Cotton / Acrylic in Baffle)
Airflow_Conditions: Forced airflow between parallel plates 5 to 20 cm/s
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Flames propagated in narrow 10 mm channel gap
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR video suite, thermocouple array, heat flux sensors
Key_Findings: Radiative heat feedback from adjacent baffle walls in narrow spacecraft rack geometries accelerated flame spread and trapped combustion products in confined channels compared to open-space configurations.
AI_Research_Summary: Demonstrated that fires inside narrow equipment racks and crawl spaces spread faster than in open cabin rooms because the heat radiating off nearby walls is trapped and bounces back onto the fuel.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Directly impacts avionics rack safety: tightly packed electrical equipment bays require non-combustible internal insulation and localized aspirated smoke detectors rather than relying on room-level sensors.
Source_Notes: Investigated flame spread in confined spaces between parallel baffle plates aboard the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack in 2019.

Airflow_Conditions: Quiescent with variable diluent gas (CO2, N2, He)
Flame_Spread_Measurement: N/A (Droplet combustion kinetics, not surface spread)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Extinction limits measured across multiple suppressants
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: CIR Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus, radiometers, imaging
Key_Findings: Confirmed cool-flame phenomenon across an expanded droplet size range and fuel mixture set; suppression agents showed altered extinction effectiveness in microgravity due to absence of buoyant gas-phase mixing.
AI_Research_Summary: Expanded on FLEX by testing how different fire extinguisher gases (CO2, nitrogen, helium) extinguish flames in space without gravity-driven gas mixing.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Proves that fire extinguishing tactics developed for Earth do not behave identically in microgravity; optimal suppression agent delivery requires tailored spacecraft protocols and continuous atmosphere verification.
Source_Notes: Conducted on the ISS between 2013 and 2014 as the second campaign of the Flame Extinguishment Experiment.

Fuel_Type: Solid Materials (Nylon, Velcro, Foam, Wire Insulation)
Extinction_Limit_Observation: Fatal flashover at 100% O2 cabin atmosphere
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Post-accident telemetry, pressure sensors, forensic teardown
Key_Findings: A 100% pure oxygen environment at 16.7 psi turned ordinary cabin materials explosively flammable, causing fatal flashover within 17 seconds following an electrical arc during a pre-launch test.
AI_Research_Summary: Historical catastrophic accident: a pure oxygen environment caused an electrical spark to turn everyday cabin items into an uncontrollable inferno, leading to the loss of astronauts Grissom, White, and Chaffee.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Prompted the complete overhaul of spacecraft atmosphere design: NASA eliminated 100% oxygen ground operations, mandated mixed nitrogen-oxygen atmospheres, and established standardized flammability testing.
Source_Notes: Ground test accident on Launch Complex 34. Historical context entry; excluded from quantitative microgravity experiment comparisons.

Extinction_Limit_Observation: Self-contained chemical reaction; burned without cabin O2
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Station air monitoring, post-incident cosmonaut reports
Key_Findings: A solid-fuel perchlorate oxygen candle ignited unexpectedly, burning for 14 minutes and filling the Mir station with dense, acrid smoke and molten metal slag, blocking one of two Soyuz emergency return craft.
AI_Research_Summary: Historical in-flight emergency: a chemical oxygen-generating canister caught fire aboard Mir, creating a 14-minute blowtorch that filled the module with blinding toxic smoke and threatened station abandonment.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Prompted space station safety redesign: the ISS utilizes water-electrolysis oxygen generation rather than chemical candles as the primary system, and mandates multiple unobstructed egress routes at all times.
DOI_Or_Reference: NASA History Division Mir Fire Analysis
Source_Notes: In-flight emergency aboard the Russian Mir space station on February 23, 1997. Historical context entry; excluded from quantitative experiment comparisons.

Extinction_Limit_Observation: Teflon wire combustion in supercritical pure O2
Sensors_And_Diagnostics: Pressure transducers, electrical telemetry, flight logs
Key_Findings: Damaged Teflon wire insulation sparked inside cryogenic oxygen tank 2, causing an electrical arc that ignited the insulation and ruptured the tank, crippling the Service Module life support and electrical power.
AI_Research_Summary: Historical in-flight emergency: an electrical spark inside a liquid oxygen tank caused a catastrophic explosion 200,000 miles from Earth; the crew survived by using the Lunar Module as an emergency lifeboat.
Potential_Spacecraft_Relevance: Led to the total redesign of spacecraft cryogenic systems: elimination of internal electrical wiring in oxygen tanks, addition of isolated auxiliary batteries, and implementation of independent safe-haven protocols.
Source_Notes: In-flight cryogenic tank rupture occurring April 13, 1970 en route to the Moon. Historical context entry; excluded from quantitative experiment comparisons.
